name: Lowering pitch exercises
lead: Lowering pitch exercises are vocal practices that people use to speak at a lower fundamental frequency, usually to sound deeper, calmer or more masculine. They appear in looksmaxxing discussion of voice as a way to change a perceived trait without surgery or drugs. The aim is auditory rather than visual: a lower, steadier voice that listeners associate with a larger, more dominant speaker.

Pitch depends on how quickly the vocal folds vibrate, which in turn depends on fold length, mass and tension. Longer, larger folds vibrate more slowly, and adult male folds are longer than adult female folds.[1] Typical adult male speech fundamentals are reported between about 90 and 155 Hz and female between about 165 and 255 Hz.[2] Habitual speaking pitch within a person's range can shift with tension, breath support and speaking habits, which is the space these exercises work in.

Research on listener responses reports that lower male pitch is associated with perceived attractiveness, physical strength and dominance, and with preference for leaders [5][6]. No published clinical studies were found that test lowering-pitch exercises in healthy speakers for appearance purposes.

paras: Practitioners describe gliding down from a comfortable pitch, humming, and reading aloud at a lower target pitch. These resemble pitch-range exercises used in speech-language pathology, such as the stretching exercises in REST, which glide the voice through a range from a comfortable pitch.[3]

Related techniques come from speech-language pathology: Wikipedia's voice therapy article lists resonant voice therapy (humming and 'Y-Buzz' exercises that use minimally closed vocal folds), range-expansion exercises (REST), vocal function exercises that glide the voice low to high and high to low, and semi-occluded methods such as straw phonation that encourage efficient voicing with less forceful fold vibration [3]. Voice therapy is delivered by speech-language pathologists [3].
Voice masculinisation or feminisation training for transgender clients includes deliberate changes to pitch and resonance, which the voice therapy article treats as a separate clinical use [3].

Laryngeal muscles adjust fold length and tension to tune pitch. Vocal fold size sets the lower and upper limits of an individual's range, and the larger male vocal tract mostly shapes timbre independently of the folds.[1]
Vocal pedagogy sources describe teachers starting students in a comfortable middle range and expanding range gradually, rather than forcing extremes.[4]

The fundamental frequency of a voice is the lowest repeating rate of vocal fold vibration, and listeners perceive pitch even when the fundamental itself is weak because harmonics create the impression of a tone [2]. Resonance (the shape of the throat and mouth) shapes timbre separately from pitch, so a voice can sound deeper through both a lower fundamental and lower resonance [1].

Studies of listener responses report associations between male voice pitch and social impressions. In a 2012 experiment by Anderson and Klofstad, men preferred a lower-pitched voice (about 20 Hz lower) for both male and female candidates in hypothetical elections for school board member and PTO president, while women preferred lower-pitched female candidates but did not distinguish between higher- and lower-pitched male candidates [5]. The authors cite earlier work finding that lower-pitched male voices are rated as more attractive, physically stronger and more socially dominant [5].

A registered report analysing 135 amateur MMA fights and 189 amateur boxing fights from YouTube videos measured each fighter's pre-fight pitch and found that pitch difference did not predict who won, with correlations of 0.06 in MMA and 0.01 in boxing. The authors describe lower male pitch as consistently linked to perceived attractiveness and dominance and weakly associated with height, strength and testosterone [6].

No studies found of lowering-pitch exercises in healthy speakers for appearance purposes. Voice therapy research focuses on voice disorders and, in transgender voice therapy, on deliberate changes to overall voice quality, which is a separate clinical use.[3] Listener-perception studies of male voice pitch are summarised above and test recorded voices rather than training programmes.[5][6]

The voice therapy article notes that clients must learn exercises without straining their voice and warns against phonotrauma such as yelling and throat clearing [3]. Vocal pedagogy sources describe starting in a comfortable middle range and expanding range gradually rather than forcing extremes [4]. Because fold size sets the limits of an individual's range, a change in habitual pitch happens inside that range [1].

card.summary: Practising a lower speaking pitch for a deeper voice; physiology sets limits and no appearance trials exist.
card.note: Pitch range is set largely by vocal fold size; no trials in healthy speakers.

quick.overview:
Lowering pitch exercises are voice practices such as gliding down, humming and reading at a lower pitch, used to sound deeper.

References describe pitch as depending mainly on vocal fold length and tension. No published trials test these exercises for appearance in healthy speakers.
quick.mechanism: Laryngeal muscles adjust fold length and tension; exercises aim to make a lower habitual pitch comfortable.
quick.risks: No documented harms from gentle practice were found; pedagogy sources caution against forcing the voice beyond a comfortable range.

chain: Gliding, humming and low-pitch reading practice
Speaking pitch settles lower within the person's natural range
Voice sounds deeper and, in listener studies, lower pitch is rated as more dominant
angle.text: People practise speaking lower so that their everyday voice sounds deeper. The change is to the voice itself within the range the vocal folds allow, and listener studies describe lower male pitch as associated with perceived dominance and strength.
